prompt: Why does the course use a pharmacy rather than a bookshop as its company?
hint: Think about what an order says about the customer.

choices.text: Pharmacies are the only businesses the LGPD applies to
choices.why: No. The LGPD applies to almost every organisation that processes personal data in Brazil.

choices.text: Its orders reveal health
choices.why: which the LGPD treats as sensitive data

choices.text: A pharmacy has more customers
choices.why: No. The size of the customer list is not the point; what it reveals is.

choices.text: Bookshops hold no personal data at all
choices.why: No. A bookshop's customer list is personal data too; it is just not sensitive in the legal sense.

prompt: Why are law and technique taught together in this course rather than in separate halves?
hint: Each one leaves a gap the other fills.

choices.text: Because the exam asks about both in the same question
choices.why: No. The reason is about the data, not about the exam.

choices.text: Because the law specifies which database to use
choices.why: No. The LGPD names no technology.

choices.text: Each one is incomplete without the other
choices.why: Right. A legal basis is worth nothing if everybody reads every column, and perfect grants are still unlawful without a reason to collect.

choices.text: Because lawyers write the grants
choices.why: No. Engineers write the grants; lawyers decide what they must achieve.

prompt: Why does the course recommend building the lab in a virtual machine?
hint: Look at what lab.sh changes on the machine.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses to run on a laptop
choices.why: No. PostgreSQL runs anywhere Linux does.

choices.text: It changes users, sudo and /etc/hosts
choices.why: Right. Those are changes to keep off the computer you work on.

choices.text: The data is too large for a normal disk
choices.why: No. The data is a few megabytes.

choices.text: The platform provides the virtual machine
choices.why: No. The platform gives you no machine; you build the lab yourself.

prompt: `psql -h db.ipe.example` reaches the wrong cluster on a machine where `psql` alone reaches `gov`. What is missing?
hint: A connection by host name does not ask Ubuntu's wrapper which cluster to use.

choices.text: A line in pg_hba.conf for the host name
choices.why: No. pg_hba.conf decides who may connect once the connection reaches the right server; this one reaches the wrong port.

choices.text: A certificate for db.ipe.example
choices.why: No. A certificate is about proving the server's name, not about which port the client tries.

choices.text: PGPORT=5433 in the environment
choices.why: Right. Without it the client tries the default port, 5432, which is the main cluster.

choices.text: The user_clusters file
choices.why: No. That file is what makes plain psql work; it is not consulted for a connection by host name.

prompt: Match each message to the gate that produced it.
hint: A FATAL closes the connection; an ERROR leaves the session open.

pairs.right: authentication: the server does not know the name
authentication: the proof offered did not fit

pairs.left: ERROR: permission denied for schema sales
pairs.right: authorisation: no USAGE on the schema

pairs.left: ERROR: permission denied for table customers
pairs.right: authorisation: no SELECT on the table

prompt: A team has careful grants on every table, but every role's password is kept in a shared spreadsheet. What is wrong?
hint: The grants are checked against a name. Who can claim it?

choices.text: Whoever holds the sheet is any role
choices.why: Right. The grants protect a name, not a person: authorisation is only as good as the authentication that proves the name.

choices.text: Nothing; grants are what protect the data
choices.why: No. Grants are checked against whoever proved the name, and here anybody can.

choices.text: The spreadsheet should be encrypted with a stronger cipher
choices.why: No. A better-locked list of shared passwords is still shared passwords.

choices.text: The grants should be on schemas instead of tables
choices.why: No. The level of the grant is not the problem.

prompt: In PostgreSQL, what makes a role a "user" rather than a "group"?
hint: It is one attribute.

choices.text: A separate CREATE USER table
choices.why: No. CREATE USER exists, but it is CREATE ROLE with LOGIN; there is one kind of principal.

choices.text: The LOGIN attribute
choices.why: Right. A role that may log in is a user; one that may not is used as a group.

choices.text: Having a password
choices.why: No. A role can log in by peer or certificate with no password at all.

choices.text: Being a member of another role
choices.why: No. Membership is how groups work, but a user can be a member too.

prompt: Ana is granted `ipe_owner` `WITH INHERIT FALSE`. What does she have to do before she can alter a table owned by `ipe_owner`?
hint: The privileges do not flow to her on their own.

choices.text: Log in again as ipe_owner
choices.why: No. ipe_owner cannot log in at all.

choices.text: Ask the superuser to run the change
choices.why: No. She has the membership; she only has to use it.

choices.text: SET ROLE ipe_owner
choices.why: Right. The change is then made under that name, deliberately.

choices.text: Nothing; membership is enough
choices.why: No. With INHERIT FALSE, membership gives her the right to become the role, not its privileges.

prompt: The website and the nightly pipeline share one role, `ipe_app`. Lesson 10 needs to know who read the prescriptions table on 3 May. What can it say?
hint: An audit trail records a role.

choices.text: Which of the two programs it was, worked out from the time of each read
choices.why: No. Both programs can run at any time; a timestamp is a guess, not an attribution.

choices.text: Only that ipe_app did, which is one of two programs
choices.why: Right. One role per program is what turns a log line into an answer.

choices.text: Nothing, because programs are never logged
choices.why: No. Program connections are logged like any other; the role just does not say which program.

choices.text: The exact process that read each row
choices.why: No. A shared role cannot tell the two apart.

prompt: Why does Ana set passwords with `\password` rather than `ALTER ROLE … PASSWORD '…'`?
hint: Look at what the log printed.

choices.text: ALTER ROLE refuses to set a password on a role that has one
choices.why: No. It sets one either way, and the log shows it did.

choices.text: \password makes the password stronger by adding random characters
choices.why: No. The password is whatever was typed; what changes is where it travels.

choices.text: The client sends a verifier, so the password reaches no log
choices.why: Right. The statement sent the password as text, and the DDL log kept it.

choices.text: Only the superuser may use ALTER ROLE, and Ana is not one
choices.why: No. Ana ran it as herself and it worked.

prompt: Match each part of `SCRAM-SHA-256$4096:<a>$<b>:<c>` to what it is.
hint: One part makes it slow, one makes it unique.

pairs.right: the stored key and the server key

prompt: An auditor finds that some roles in an old cluster have a stored password starting with `md5`. Why does that matter more than a weak password policy?
hint: What would somebody holding a copy of pg_authid be able to do?

choices.text: MD5 hashes are longer, so they fill the disk
choices.why: No. Size is not the issue.

choices.text: The md5 hash itself is enough to log in
choices.why: Right. A stolen catalogue is then a stolen set of logins: a SCRAM verifier has to be attacked by guessing, an md5 hash is replayed as it is.

choices.text: MD5 roles cannot connect over TCP
choices.why: No. They can, and that is part of the problem.

choices.text: PostgreSQL 16 silently converts them
choices.why: No. Nothing converts a stored hash; the password has to be set again.

prompt: The random value stored with a SCRAM verifier, so that two people with the same password store different strings, is called the ___.
hint: It is also used in cooking.

prompt: What does the `peer` method check?
hint: It asks somebody other than the client.

choices.text: A password sent over the socket, which the server then hashes
choices.why: No. peer asks for no password at all.

choices.text: Which OS user is on the socket
choices.why: Right. The kernel says who is on the other end, and the role has to have the same name.

choices.text: A certificate signed by the lab's own certificate authority
choices.why: No. That is the cert method, over TCP with TLS.

choices.text: That the client's IP address is 127.0.0.1, the machine itself
choices.why: No. A socket has no IP address; the address column is for host lines.

prompt: Put the steps of changing pg_hba.conf safely in order.
hint: The server does not read the file on every edit.
trap: Skipping the last step is how a broken edit fails silently: the server keeps the last file it could parse.
items: Install it where the cluster reads it

prompt: During an incident somebody adds `host all all 0.0.0.0/0 trust` as the FIRST rule of Ana's file and forgets it. What changes?
hint: First match wins.

choices.text: Nothing, because the reject line still refuses everybody else
choices.why: No. The reject line is never read: the first line already matched.

choices.text: Only connections from outside the machine are affected
choices.why: No. 0.0.0.0/0 matches every IPv4 address, including this machine's.

choices.text: Any TCP client claims any role, no password
choices.why: Right. trust believes the name, and nothing after the first match is read.

choices.text: The superuser alone can still connect
choices.why: No. It opens the door for every role, not only postgres.

prompt: A connection matches no line at all. Why add an explicit `reject` line at the end, if the connection is refused either way?
hint: Compare the two messages in the log.

choices.text: It makes refusals faster
choices.why: No. The difference is not speed.

choices.text: It changes the reason in the log
choices.why: Right. A rule refused it, rather than no rule matched: a deliberate refusal reads differently from a file that was perhaps edited wrongly.

choices.text: Without it unmatched connections are let in
choices.why: No. A connection that matches no line is refused.

choices.text: PostgreSQL requires the last line to be reject
choices.why: No. It is a choice, not a requirement.

prompt: With `~/.pgpass` readable by every user on the machine, what does libpq do?
hint: Read the warning.

choices.text: Uses it and logs a warning on the server
choices.why: No. The server never knows; the client refuses on its own.

choices.text: Fixes the permissions itself
choices.why: No. It changes nothing on disk.

choices.text: Deletes the file
choices.why: No. Nothing is deleted.

choices.text: Ignores it and asks at a prompt
choices.why: Right. It warns, then falls back to asking, and with no terminal it gives up.

prompt: Why does the server answer a role that does not exist with the same message as a wrong password?
hint: What would a different message let a stranger find out?

choices.text: So the login cannot be used to find out which roles exist
choices.why: Right. The real reason goes to the server's log, where only the people who run it read it.

choices.text: Because the server does not know the reason itself
choices.why: No. The log shows it knows exactly.

choices.text: To save bandwidth
choices.why: No. The messages are the same length either way.

choices.text: Because the role is created automatically on the first attempt
choices.why: No. Nothing is created.

prompt: In the lab, Ana's `~/.pgpass` holds the passwords of six roles. Why would that be a defect in a real company even with mode 0600?
hint: Think about what a log line saying `bruno` would then mean.

choices.text: The file format allows one line only
choices.why: No. It holds one line per server, port, database and role.

choices.text: Mode 0600 is not enough; it should be 0400
choices.why: No. 0600 is what libpq asks for; the problem is not the mode.

choices.text: A log line saying bruno might mean Ana
choices.why: Right. The role stops identifying a person: shared knowledge of a password breaks attribution even when the file is safe.

choices.text: libpq refuses a file with more than one role in it
choices.why: No. It reads as many lines as the file has.

prompt: Lia's role was created `VALID UNTIL '2026-06-30'`. What happens on 1 July if nobody does anything?
hint: That is the point of writing the date down.

choices.text: The role is dropped
choices.why: No. The role and its grants remain; only the password stops working.

choices.text: Her password stops working
choices.why: Right. The log records the reason: an expired password.

choices.text: She is asked to choose a new password at the next login
choices.why: No. PostgreSQL has no such prompt; the login is refused.

choices.text: Nothing until an administrator runs a job
choices.why: No. The expiry is checked at every login, by the server.

prompt: Which of these still let Lia's role reach data after her password has expired? Choose all that apply.
hint: VALID UNTIL is about the password and nothing else.

choices.text: A pg_hba.conf rule letting her in by certificate
choices.why: Yes. A certificate login does not use the password.

choices.text: A pg_hba.conf rule letting her in by peer
choices.why: Yes. peer asks the operating system, not the password.

choices.text: A scram-sha-256 rule for her address
choices.why: No. That method checks the password, which has expired.

choices.text: Her entry in Ana's ~/.pgpass
choices.why: No. The file supplies the expired password, which the server refuses.

prompt: `site_app` was created with `CONNECTION LIMIT 3`. Three connections are open. How many more can it open?
hint: The fourth was refused.

prompt: Why does a connection limit belong on `site_app` and not on Bruno?
hint: Think about what opens connections in a loop.

choices.text: Because people cannot open more than one connection
choices.why: No. A person can open as many windows as they like.

choices.text: Because the limit only works on service accounts
choices.why: No. It works on any role; the question is where it is useful.

choices.text: A bug opens connections without end
choices.why: Right. A person opening a fourth window is not a fault; a program looping is, and the limit makes the leak hurt the website rather than everybody.

choices.text: Because Bruno is an analyst and analysts need more memory
choices.why: No. Memory per connection is the same for everybody.

prompt: Put the steps of removing a departed person's access in order.
hint: Stop new sessions first; keep what they created; then remove the rest.
items: REASSIGN OWNED BY lia TO ipe_owner

prompt: What does single sign-on change about offboarding?
hint: Count the places an account has to be closed.

choices.text: Disabling the account at the identity provider closes every door at once
choices.why: Right. One action instead of a checklist per system.

choices.text: People no longer need accounts at all
choices.why: No. They still have one, at the identity provider.

choices.text: It removes the need for grants
choices.why: No. SSO is authentication; what the person may read is still decided by grants.

choices.text: Service accounts are closed automatically too
choices.why: No. Service accounts have no person to sign in and are outside the provider's offboarding.

prompt: Match each method to how it proves who the client is.
hint: One sends no password, one asks a directory, one uses a key pair.

pairs.right: the database asks a directory server to check the password
a ticket from a Kerberos realm
a private key the company's CA signed
the operating system names the user on the socket

prompt: A company says all data access requires MFA through its identity provider. Where should an access review look first?
hint: What does the provider's offboarding not reach?

choices.text: At the provider's own password policy
choices.why: No. That is the part already covered by MFA.

choices.text: At service accounts and local passwords
choices.why: Right. They never pass through the provider, so they are the doors without a second factor.

choices.text: At the BI tool
choices.why: No. The BI tool signs in through the provider, so it is the covered case.

choices.text: At the VPN, because MFA cannot work there
choices.why: No. A VPN is one of the usual places MFA is enforced.

prompt: After `log_connections = on`, what does a successful login leave in the log?
hint: Two lines.

choices.text: Nothing; successes are never logged
choices.why: No. That was the state before the setting.

choices.text: The password that was used
choices.why: No. The password is never logged at login.

choices.text: Its identity and method, then what it opened
choices.why: Right. Method and rule, then database, application and encryption.

choices.text: Every statement the session runs from then on
choices.why: No. That is a different setting, and lesson 10's pgaudit.

prompt: The log shows `etl_loader` connecting at 14:12 with `application_name=psql`. The pipeline runs at 03:00. What is the likeliest explanation?
hint: Which program calls itself psql?

choices.text: The pipeline was rescheduled
choices.why: No. The pipeline would not name itself psql.

choices.text: A clock error in the log
choices.why: No. Nothing else in the log suggests one.

choices.text: The connection limit was reached
choices.why: No. A refused connection would not appear as authorised.

choices.text: A person is using the pipeline's password interactively
choices.why: Right. A service account used by a person is one of the questions this log exists to answer.

prompt: Carla's connection was logged as `SSL enabled`, though nobody in lesson 1 configured TLS. Why?
hint: Look at who created the cluster.

choices.text: Ubuntu's packaging made a certificate
choices.why: Right. Ubuntu turns TLS on for new clusters with a certificate generated on the spot, one no client is able to verify, which is where lesson 3 starts.

choices.text: PostgreSQL encrypts every connection by default on every system
choices.why: No. That is Ubuntu's packaging, not PostgreSQL's own default.

choices.text: Carla's password is encrypted with SCRAM
choices.why: No. SCRAM protects the password exchange; SSL in that line is the whole connection.

choices.text: The lab's certificate authority signed a certificate for the server
choices.why: No. The lab's CA exists, but lesson 3 is where it is used.

prompt: What is `PUBLIC` in PostgreSQL?
hint: Every role is in it.

choices.text: The schema called public
choices.why: No. Same word, different thing: the schema is an object, PUBLIC is a pseudo-role.

choices.text: A pseudo-role every role belongs to, including roles created later
choices.why: Right. A grant to PUBLIC is a grant to everybody, now and in future.

choices.text: The role anonymous web visitors use
choices.why: No. PostgreSQL has no notion of a web visitor.

choices.text: A superuser alias
choices.why: No. PUBLIC has only what has been granted to it.

prompt: Bruno can log in but cannot read `sales.customers`. What can he still see?
hint: Every client needs it to work.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: No. \dn worked for him.

choices.text: The first ten rows of each table
choices.why: No. There is no such preview.

choices.text: The catalogue, not the rows
choices.why: Right. Schema, table and column names and the other roles, which is why a revealing table name is a leak whatever its grants say.

choices.text: Row counts but not values
choices.why: No. count(*) was refused at the schema.

prompt: Somebody extends Lia's password by mistake. Why can she still not open a session on `ipe`?
hint: There is a second control, made by somebody not doing something.

choices.text: Her row in pg_hba.conf was removed
choices.why: No. Line 4 still matches her.

choices.text: CONNECT was revoked from PUBLIC and never granted to her
choices.why: Right. Two independent controls: one would have to fail and the other be undone.

choices.text: Expired passwords cannot be extended
choices.why: No. ALTER ROLE can change VALID UNTIL at any time.

choices.text: Her connection limit is zero
choices.why: No. Nobody set one on her role.

prompt: Put the checks a connection to `ipe` goes through in order, first to last.
hint: The door, then the room, then the shelf.
items: The first matching line of pg_hba.conf picks a method
CONNECT on the database is checked
USAGE on the schema is checked, at the first statement

prompt: A new analyst role is created with a password, and the first thing it does is read `sales.customers` successfully. Which default must still be in place?
hint: In Ana's lab this would fail at two places.

choices.text: The peer rule in pg_hba.conf
choices.why: No. peer is about the socket and the operating-system user, not about reading tables.

choices.text: password_encryption = scram-sha-256
choices.why: No. That decides how a password is stored, not what a role may read.

choices.text: Grants made to PUBLIC
choices.why: Right. CONNECT on the database and access to the schema and table: a brand-new role reads only what PUBLIC reads.

choices.text: VALID UNTIL infinity
choices.why: No. Expiry decides when a password stops working, not what it opens.

prompt: In pg_hba.conf the server stops reading at the ___ line that matches the connection.
hint: Order is a security property.
